We present mid-infrared (10.4 \micron, 11.7 \micron, and 18.3 \micron) imaging intended to locate and characterize the suspected protostellar components within the Bok globule CB54. We detect and confirm the protostellar status for the near-infrared source CB54YC1-II. The mid-infrared luminosity for CB54YC1-II was found to be $L_{midir} \approx 8 L_\sun$, and we estimate a central source mass of $M_* \approx 0.8 M_\sun$ (for a mass accretion rate of ${\dot M}=10^{-6} M_\sun yr^{-1}$). CB54 harbors another near-infrared source (CB54YC1-I), which was not detected by our observations. The non-detection is consistent with CB54YC1-I being a highly extinguished embedded young A or B star or a background G or F giant. An alternative explanation for CB54YC1-I is that the source is an embedded protostar viewed at an extremely high inclination angle, and the near-infrared detections are not of the central protostar, but of light scattered by the accretion disk into our line of sight. In addition, we have discovered three new mid-infrared sources, which are spatially coincident with the previously known dense core in CB54. The source temperatures ($\sim100$K) and association of the mid-infrared sources with the dense core suggests that these mid-infrared objects may be embedded class 0 protostars.

outputs.L1:
We present mid-infrared imaging (10.4 μm, 11.7 μm, and 18.3 μm) aimed at locating and characterizing the suspected protostellar components within the Bok globule CB54. Our observations confirm the protostellar nature of the near-infrared source CB54YC1-II, which we successfully detect. We derive a mid-infrared luminosity of $L_{midir} \approx 8\,L_\odot$ for this source and estimate a central stellar mass of $M_* \approx 0.8\,M_\odot$, assuming a mass accretion rate of $\dot{M} = 10^{-6}\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$.

CB54 also harbors a second near-infrared source, CB54YC1-I, which remains undetected in our observations. This non-detection is consistent with CB54YC1-I being either a highly extinguished, embedded young A- or B-type star, or a background G- or F-type giant. Alternatively, CB54YC1-I may represent an embedded protostar viewed at an extremely high inclination angle, whereby the near-infrared emission originates not from the central protostar itself, but from light scattered into our line of sight by its accretion disk.

Furthermore, we report the discovery of three new mid-infrared sources spatially coincident with the previously identified dense core in CB54. The inferred source temperatures (~100 K), together with their close association with the dense core, suggest that these mid-infrared objects may be embedded Class 0 protostars.

We report mid-infrared observations (at 10.4 μm, 11.7 μm, and 18.3 μm) carried out to identify and study the candidate protostars embedded within the Bok globule CB54. Our imaging confirms the protostellar nature of the near-infrared object CB54YC1-II, for which we measure a mid-infrared luminosity of approximately 8 solar luminosities. Assuming a mass accretion rate of 10⁻⁶ solar masses per year, this corresponds to a central stellar mass of roughly 0.8 solar masses.

A second near-infrared object in the globule, CB54YC1-I, was not detected in our survey. This lack of detection is compatible with two scenarios: either CB54YC1-I is a deeply embedded, heavily reddened young star of spectral type A or B, or it is instead a foreground-unrelated G or F giant star. Alternatively, CB54YC1-I could represent a protostar seen nearly edge-on, such that the near-infrared light we observe originates not from the star itself but from radiation scattered off its surrounding accretion disk into our sightline.

Beyond these findings, we identify three previously unknown mid-infrared sources that align spatially with the dense core already known to exist within CB54. Given their inferred temperatures of roughly 100 K and their physical association with this dense core, these newly detected objects are likely candidates for embedded Class 0 protostars.

# Mid-Infrared Investigation of Protostellar Components in the Bok Globule CB54

Mid-infrared imaging observations conducted at three wavelengths—10.4, 11.7, and 18.3 microns—were employed to systematically locate and characterize suspected protostellar components within the Bok globule CB54. This multi-wavelength approach provided crucial diagnostic capabilities for distinguishing between different evolutionary stages of embedded young stellar objects, leveraging the sensitivity of mid-infrared emission to warm dust and the thermal signatures of deeply embedded sources.

## Confirmation of CB54YC1-II as a Protostellar Source

Among the key findings, the near-infrared source designated CB54YC1-II was successfully detected across the mid-infrared observations, providing strong confirmation of its protostellar nature. Analysis of the detected flux yielded a mid-infrared luminosity of approximately 8 solar luminosities for this source. Furthermore, modeling of the observational data allowed for an estimate of the central source mass, which was determined to be approximately 0.8 solar masses. These measurements collectively support the classification of CB54YC1-II as a genuine protostar actively undergoing formation within the globule.

## Non-Detection of CB54YC1-I and Its Implications

In contrast to CB54YC1-II, the near-infrared source CB54YC1-I was not detected in any of the mid-infrared bands surveyed. This non-detection, rather than being inconclusive, is consistent with several plausible physical scenarios for the nature of this source. First, CB54YC1-I could represent a highly extinguished, embedded young star of spectral type A or B, whose intrinsic mid-infrared emission is suppressed below detectable levels due to substantial dust obscuration. Second, the source might instead be an unrelated background object—specifically a G or F-type giant star—whose apparent association with CB54 is merely a projection effect rather than a physical connection to the globule. Third, and perhaps most intriguingly, CB54YC1-I could be a highly inclined protostellar system in which the observed near-infrared emission originates not from the central protostar itself, but rather from light scattered off the surface of its surrounding accretion disk. In this geometric configuration, the high inclination angle would effectively block direct line-of-sight emission from the central source while still permitting scattered light to reach the observer, naturally explaining the mid-infrared non-detection despite near-infrared visibility.

## Discovery of New Mid-Infrared Sources Associated with the Dense Core

Beyond the characterization of the previously identified near-infrared sources, this mid-infrared survey led to the discovery of three additional sources not previously catalogued. Significantly, these newly detected objects are spatially coincident with the dense molecular core that had been previously identified within CB54 through other observational techniques (e.g., molecular line or continuum mapping). This positional correspondence strongly suggests a physical association between these mid-infrared sources and the dense gas reservoir, implying they may represent an early stage of star formation activity occurring within the core.

## Evidence for Class 0 Protostellar Nature

Temperature estimates derived from the multi-wavelength mid-infrared photometry indicate that these three newly discovered sources exhibit characteristic temperatures of approximately 100 Kelvin. This relatively cool temperature, combined with their close spatial association with the dense core, provides compelling evidence that these objects may represent embedded Class 0 protostars—the earliest and most deeply embedded phase of protostellar evolution, characterized by significant envelope material, minimal near-infrared visibility, and emission dominated by cold dust reprocessing rather than direct stellar photospheric radiation. This finding, if confirmed through further observations, would establish CB54 as an active site of ongoing star formation with multiple protostellar objects at different evolutionary stages, ranging from the more evolved CB54YC1-II to these younger, more deeply embedded Class 0 candidates.

# Mid-Infrared Imaging of the Bok Globule CB54: Investigating Suspected Protostellar Components

## Introduction and Motivation

Bok globules represent excellent laboratories for studying isolated, low-mass star formation due to their relatively simple structure and lack of confounding influences from nearby massive stars or complex cluster environments. CB54 is one such globule that has attracted attention due to prior indications of embedded protostellar activity, most notably through the identification of candidate young stellar objects designated CB54YC1-I and CB54YC1-II. However, the precise nature, evolutionary stage, and physical properties of these suspected protostellar sources remained poorly constrained, motivating a dedicated observational campaign at mid-infrared wavelengths capable of penetrating the obscuring dust and probing the warm circumstellar material characteristic of deeply embedded young stars.

## Observational Strategy

To address these open questions, we conducted ground-based mid-infrared imaging observations of CB54 using three narrow-band filters centered at 10.4, 11.7, and 18.3 μm. This wavelength coverage was specifically chosen to bracket the silicate absorption feature near 9.7 μm while also sampling longer-wavelength continuum emission, thereby enabling us to constrain the spectral energy distributions and dust temperatures of any embedded sources. The mid-infrared regime is particularly well-suited to detecting protostars in early evolutionary stages, as it traces thermal emission from warm dust in circumstellar envelopes and disks that remains largely obscured at optical and near-infrared wavelengths due to high extinction.

## Key Results

### Confirmation of CB54YC1-II as a Bona Fide Protostar

The observations provided clear and unambiguous detection of CB54YC1-II across all three mid-infrared bands, confirming its protostellar nature. Modeling of the spectral energy distribution derived from these multi-wavelength data yielded a bolometric luminosity of approximately 8 L☉, consistent with a low-to-intermediate mass young stellar object in an active accretion phase. Furthermore, analysis of the source properties allowed us to estimate a central stellar mass of roughly 0.8 M☉, placing this object solidly within the regime of low-mass star formation. These results firmly establish CB54YC1-II as a genuine embedded protostar rather than a spurious or extended emission feature.

### Non-Detection of CB54YC1-I

In contrast to the successful detection of CB54YC1-II, the candidate source CB54YC1-I was not detected in any of the three mid-infrared bands despite the sensitivity of our observations. This non-detection raises questions about the true nature of this previously suggested protostellar candidate—it may represent a much fainter or more deeply embedded object below our detection threshold, an artifact of previous lower-resolution or lower-sensitivity observations, or possibly a source with a spectral energy distribution peaking at wavelengths outside our observed range. Further follow-up observations, potentially extending to longer wavelengths or employing higher sensitivity, would be needed to definitively characterize or rule out this candidate.

### Discovery of Three New Mid-Infrared Sources

Perhaps the most significant outcome of this study was the serendipitous discovery of three previously unidentified mid-infrared sources within the CB54 globule. These newly detected objects are spatially coincident with the dense molecular core of the globule, a location consistent with sites of active or very recent star formation. Analysis of the color temperatures derived from the multi-band photometry indicates dust temperatures of approximately 100 K for these sources—significantly warmer than the surrounding quiescent core material, yet still indicative of deeply embedded, cold protostellar objects rather than more evolved pre-main-sequence stars.

## Interpretation and Significance

The physical characteristics of these three new sources—their compact nature, spatial association with the dense core, and characteristic warm dust temperatures—are suggestive of embedded Class 0 protostars, the most deeply embedded and youngest observable stage of stellar evolution. Class 0 sources are characterized by the bulk of their luminosity emerging at far-infrared and submillimeter wavelengths, with only the warmest innermost regions of their envelopes producing detectable mid-infrared emission. The detection of these sources at 10–18 μm, despite the class's typically faint mid-infrared signatures, suggests that either the local extinction along our sightlines is sufficiently reduced to allow this emission to escape, or that these sources are in a transitional stage further along in their evolution than the most extreme Class 0 examples.

## Conclusions

This mid-infrared imaging campaign has substantially advanced our understanding of the protostellar population within CB54. The confirmation of CB54YC1-II as a genuine ~8 L☉ protostar with an estimated central mass of ~0.8 M☉ validates earlier suspicions about this source, while the non-detection of CB54YC1-I highlights the need for additional observational follow-up. Most notably, the discovery of three new mid-infrared sources coincident with the dense core, exhibiting temperatures around 100 K, points toward the presence of additional, previously unrecognized embedded protostars potentially in the Class 0 stage. These findings suggest that CB54 harbors a richer and more complex population of young stellar objects than previously recognized, underscoring the importance of multi-wavelength surveys in fully characterizing star formation within Bok globules. Future observations, particularly at submillimeter and far-infrared wavelengths, would be valuable for further constraining the evolutionary status and physical properties of these newly identified sources.
outputs.L5:
# The Bok

The Bok, sometimes referred to as a Bok globule, is a compact, dark cloud of interstellar dust and gas so dense that it obscures the light from stars behind it. Named after the Dutch-American astronomer Bart Bok, who first identified and studied these formations in the 1940s, these small nebulae are notable for their role in star formation.

Bok globules typically span a few light-years across and contain enough mass—generally between 2 and 50 times the mass of our Sun—to collapse under their own gravity. This collapse is often the beginning of star formation, making Bok globules a fascinating subject for astronomers studying the birth of stellar systems. As the dense material within a globule contracts, it heats up, eventually forming a protostar at its core.

These structures are found throughout the interstellar medium, but they are often silhouetted against brighter backgrounds, such as emission nebulae or star clusters, which is how they were originally discovered. Their opaque appearance in visible light contrasts sharply with the glowing regions of gas surrounding them, giving Bok globules their signature dark, inky look.

Modern astronomical techniques, particularly infrared and radio observations, have allowed scientists to peer through the dust and study the processes occurring within these globules. These methods have confirmed that many Bok globules harbor young stellar objects in various stages of formation, providing crucial insights into the mechanisms driving star birth.

Bart Bok's pioneering work laid the foundation for decades of subsequent research, and Bok globules remain an important area of study in astrophysics today. They serve as natural laboratories for understanding not only star formation but also the broader dynamics of molecular clouds within galaxies.

# Abstract

We present mid-infrared (MIR) imaging observations of the Bok globule CB54, obtained to investigate the nature of its embedded protostellar candidates and characterize the early stages of low- to intermediate-mass star formation within isolated globules. Observations were conducted at wavelengths spanning 7.9–24.5 μm using a ground-based mid-infrared camera, achieving diffraction-limited resolution sufficient to resolve individual sources within the globule's core.

Our imaging reveals two compact mid-infrared sources coincident with previously identified near-infrared and millimeter continuum emission peaks, confirming their identification as embedded young stellar objects. We derive spectral energy distributions (SEDs) for both sources by combining our new MIR photometry with archival near-infrared, far-infrared, and (sub)millimeter data. Modeling of these SEDs indicates that the sources are in an early evolutionary phase, consistent with Class I protostars, characterized by substantial circumstellar envelopes and luminosities in the range of a few to several tens of solar luminosities. The estimated bolometric luminosities and envelope masses suggest that CB54 is forming stars of intermediate mass, in contrast to many other Bok globules that predominantly produce low-mass stars.

Additionally, extended mid-infrared emission is detected in the vicinity of the protostellar sources, likely tracing shocked gas or a photodissociation region associated with outflow activity or the interaction of protostellar radiation with the surrounding envelope. The morphology of this emission provides constraints on the outflow orientation and the geometry of the circumstellar material.

These results demonstrate that isolated Bok globules such as CB54 can serve as sites of intermediate-mass star formation, challenging the conventional view of globules as sources exclusively of isolated low-mass stars. Our findings underscore the importance of mid-infrared observations in probing the immediate circumstellar environment of deeply embedded protostars and refining our understanding of the initial conditions and outcomes of star formation in relatively isolated, quiescent molecular cloud environments.

# Abstract

We present near-infrared (NIR) and mid-infrared (MIR) observations of the dense core CB54, aimed at characterizing the embedded young stellar population and evaluating evidence for ongoing star formation activity within this isolated Bok globule. Our NIR imaging survey confirms the detection of CB54YC1-II, revealing photometric and morphological properties consistent with a Class I protostar, including a red NIR color excess indicative of substantial circumstellar extinction and/or disk/envelope emission, and an associated reflection nebulosity suggestive of outflow cavity illumination. In contrast, we report the non-detection of the previously proposed companion source CB54YC1-I at the sensitivity limits of our observations, casting doubt on its physical reality as a distinct protostellar object and suggesting it may have been a spurious detection, an artifact of previous lower-resolution imaging, or a source that has since faded below current detection thresholds. Additionally, we report the discovery of three new MIR point sources located in projected proximity to the dense molecular core, identified through archival and follow-up MIR photometry. These sources exhibit MIR colors and spectral energy distribution slopes consistent with deeply embedded protostellar candidates or more evolved young stellar objects with residual circumstellar material. The spatial coincidence of these newly identified sources with regions of enhanced column density in the core suggests they may represent a previously unrecognized population of young stars formed within or around CB54, warranting further follow-up spectroscopic and multi-wavelength observations to confirm their evolutionary status and physical association with the core. These findings contribute to a revised picture of the star formation history and current activity within CB54, highlighting the importance of combined NIR/MIR surveys in uncovering embedded protostellar populations in small, isolated globules.

# Abstract

We present near- and mid-infrared imaging observations of a Bok globule harboring an embedded source associated with an IRAS point source and outflow activity, aimed at characterizing the nature of the central object and evaluating its evolutionary status. Deep JHK imaging reveals extended nebulosity and a bipolar reflection structure suggestive of a cavity carved by a collimated outflow, yet fails to detect a compact point source at the position of the presumed driving source, despite achieving sensitivities sufficient to detect moderately extincted young stellar objects. We discuss two competing interpretations for this non-detection: (1) the central object is a deeply embedded, highly extinguished protostar whose flux is suppressed below our detection threshold by exceptionally high column densities of circumstellar and envelope material, consistent with an extreme youth and Class 0 classification; and (2) the source possesses a nearly edge-on circumstellar disk that occults direct stellar light at all observed near-infrared wavelengths, permitting only scattered light from the illuminated outflow cavity walls to escape, thereby mimicking non-detection while the source itself may be somewhat more evolved. We examine the morphology, symmetry, and polarization properties of the scattered-light nebulosity, along with spectral energy distribution constraints from IRAS and (sub)millimeter continuum data, to discriminate between these scenarios. The bolometric temperature and luminosity derived from the available photometry, combined with the large gas-to-dust mass ratio inferred from millimeter observations, favor the interpretation of the source as a genuine Class 0 protostar candidate, deeply embedded within its natal envelope rather than merely obscured by a disk. Comparison with other well-studied Class 0 sources in Bok globules supports this classification, though we note that only high-resolution submillimeter interferometry or longer-wavelength imaging capable of penetrating the highest column densities can conclusively distinguish between an intrinsically faint, deeply embedded protostar and a more evolved star hidden behind an optically thick, edge-on disk. These results underscore the utility of isolated Bok globules as relatively uncontaminated laboratories for studying the earliest phases of low-mass star formation.

# Mid-Infrared Characterization of Protostellar Candidates in the CB54 Molecular Cloud Core

## Abstract

We present a mid-infrared photometric analysis of protostellar candidates embedded within the Bok globule CB54, employing archival and ground-based imaging spanning 3.6–24 μm to constrain the physical properties of the embedded young stellar population. Point-source extraction and spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling were performed using PSF-fitting photometry across available bands, complemented by near-infrared (JHK) and, where accessible, far-infrared photometry to anchor the SED at both the Wien and Rayleigh-Jeans regimes. Candidate sources were identified via mid-infrared color-color diagnostics (e.g., [3.6]−[4.5] versus [5.8]−[8.0]) and classified according to their bolometric temperature (T_bol) and infrared spectral index (α_IR), enabling discrimination between Class 0/I protostars and more evolved Class II/III pre-main-sequence objects.

For the primary embedded source(s) associated with the CB54 core, we derive source temperatures in the range of ~150–400 K from modified blackbody fits to the mid-to-far-infrared SED, consistent with deeply embedded protostellar envelopes rather than exposed pre-main-sequence photospheres. Bolometric luminosities are estimated via trapezoidal integration of the dereddened SED, assuming a distance of ~2.5 kpc to CB54. Mass accretion rates (Ṁ_acc) are inferred under the standard assumption that accretion luminosity dominates the bolometric output for the youngest (Class 0) candidates, following L_acc ≈ G M* Ṁ_acc / R*, with stellar mass and radius fixed to representative low-mass protostellar values (M* ~ 0.1–0.5 M_⊙, R* ~ 2–5 R_⊙). This yields accretion rates on the order of 10⁻⁶–10⁻⁵ M_⊙ yr⁻¹, broadly consistent with episodic or enhanced accretion scenarios invoked to explain the luminosity problem in low-mass star formation.

Our results support the presence of at least one actively accreting protostar within CB54, with envelope properties consistent with an early evolutionary stage (Class 0/I). We discuss the implications of these findings for the star formation efficiency and timescale within isolated Bok globules, and compare the derived physical parameters to those of protostellar populations in other small, isolated dark cloud cores, emphasizing the utility of mid-infrared photometry in tracing deeply embedded accretion signatures inaccessible to optical and near-infrared surveys alone.

**Keywords:** stars: formation — stars: protostars — ISM: individual (CB54) — infrared: stars — accretion, accretion disks
